notes: In the first test case every tile holds a $4$-opening junction, giving two independent loops (the two unit squares). Destroying tile $(1,1)$ breaks the left one and destroying tile $(1,2)$ breaks the other, hence $1\ 0\ 0$. In the second test case the eight outer junctions form a single loop around the centre, while the centre tile is connected to nothing, so removing it first changes nothing: $1\ 0$. In the third test case there are no connections at all, and in the fourth $q = 0$, so the answer line is empty.
output:
For each test case, print a single line containing $q$ integers: the $i$-th integer must be the number of independent loops remaining after the first $i$ impacts.

If $q = 0$, print an empty line.
input:
The first line contains a single integer $t$ ($1 \le t \le 2 \cdot 10^5$) --- the number of test cases.

The first line of each test case contains two integers $n$ and $m$ ($1 \le n, m$, $n \cdot m \le 2 \cdot 10^5$) --- the dimensions of the grid.

Each of the next $n$ lines contains $m$ integers $g_{i,1}, g_{i,2}, \ldots, g_{i,m}$ ($0 \le g_{i,j} \le 15$) --- the tiles of the $i$-th row, encoded as described in the statement, rows listed from top to bottom.

The next line contains a single integer $q$ ($0 \le q$) --- the number of impacts.

Each of the next $q$ lines contains two integers $r$ and $c$ ($1 \le r \le n$, $1 \le c \le m$) --- the tile destroyed by the next impact.

It is guaranteed that no tile is hit twice, that every impacted tile contains a junction, that $q$ does not exceed the number of junctions, and that the sum of $n \cdot m$ over all test cases does not exceed $2 \cdot 10^5$.
name: Impact on Polaris Deep
tutorial:
Process the impacts in reverse order: instead of deleting junctions, add them back one by one.

Start from the state after all $q$ impacts and count the active junctions $V$, the connections $E$ between them, and their connected components $C$ directly. Keep the components in a disjoint-set-union structure.

When a junction is restored, add its vertex ($V$ and $C$ increase by $1$), then look at its at most four neighbours. For every active neighbour such that the restored junction and the neighbour open towards each other, add the corresponding edge ($E$ increases by $1$); if the two endpoints were in different components, unite them ($C$ decreases by $1$).

After each restoration the number of independent loops equals $E - V + C$. Recording these values while time runs backwards and printing them in reverse order answers every impact. Each edge is considered at most once, so the running time is $O((n \cdot m + q)\, \alpha(n \cdot m))$ per test case.

Forward simulation does not work directly: deleting one junction can change the number of loops by an amount that depends on how its neighbours are connected after its removal, which is expensive to determine online.

(Why does counting with the formula $E - V + C$ match the definition in the legend? For a spanning forest of the network, every non-tree connection closes exactly one loop containing a connection no previous loop used, giving $E - V + C$ admissible loops; conversely, any loop with a fresh connection can be charged to that connection, so no sequence can be longer.)
